generation.hypothesis: An integrated, data‐driven machine learning framework used to optimize thermo‐mechanical processing can enable stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) in refractory high‐entropy alloys, concurrently enhancing both strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high‐entropy alloys processed by conventional methods that exhibit either high strength with low ductility or vice versa due to suboptimal microstructural control.
generation.intervention: Apply a machine learning–based optimization of processing parameters (e.g., rolling reduction, annealing time/temperature, aging conditions) to achieve tailored SCCPs.
generation.conditions: Ambient or standard testing conditions with thermo‐mechanical processing steps implemented under controlled laboratory settings.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoprecipitates (such as lamellar and nanoparticulate phases) that form in a stepwise manner, ensuring coherent interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The ML framework correlates processing parameters with the development of coherent precipitate microstructures that pin dislocations (enhancing strength) while facilitating dislocation transmission and local strain accommodation (preserving or improving ductility).
generation.predicted_outcome: An alloy microstructure that exhibits a simultaneous and concurrent improvement in mechanical strength and ductility relative to alloys processed by conventional, non‐optimized routes.
generation.baseline: Conventional processing without data‐driven optimization, which typically results in a trade‐off where strengthening methods reduce ductility.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be effective only in alloy systems where the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates is attainable and processing parameters can be reliably predicted by the machine learning model.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements and the direct transferability of the ML framework across different alloy systems remain to be validated, making the extent of concurrent property enhancement uncertain.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

decision.trend: Earlier studies have sought to overcome the strength–ductility trade‐off by tailoring microstructures through controlled thermo‐mechanical processing. Initial attempts involved establishing single‐phase or weakly-ordered structures that traded off strength for ductility, while subsequent work demonstrated that employing stepwise processing can generate multiple coherent precipitation structures (e.g., lamellar and nanoparticulate phases) that jointly pin dislocation motion and accommodate plasticity. These experiments showed that fine control over precipitate size, spacing, and coherency can lead to simultaneous improvements in both properties.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress, a key challenge remains in reliably and reproducibly engineering complex microstructures that concurrently maximize strength and ductility. The selection and optimization of processing parameters are still largely empirical, and the multidimensional nature of processing–structure–property relationships has hindered the systematic discovery of optimal conditions.
decision.lever: Develop an integrated, machine learning–based framework that correlates processing parameters (e.g., rolling reductions, annealing temperatures/times, aging steps) with microstructural features (e.g., coherent precipitate size/distribution) and mechanical properties.
decision.why: This lever builds on the trend of detailed experimental microstructure control and addresses the unsolved challenge of multidimensional optimization by automating the prediction and refinement of process–structure–property linkages, thereby enabling more precise concurrent improvements in both strength and ductility.
